definition: Narrative theory, in this packet, refers to a framework for understanding how presenting information as a narrative can shape audience attention, feelings, and thinking. It treats the form of a message, not just its content, as important in how people respond.

reasons: The packet does not explicitly define “narrative theory” as a framework for understanding narrative-shaped attention, feelings, and thinking; it only mentions narrative theory as an element integrated into another model (A-ELM) without giving a definition.

The definition’s claim that narrative theory treats “the form of a message, not just its content” as important is not directly supported as a description of narrative theory; the packet instead provides a general statement that linguistic presentation can affect responses even when content remains unchanged, without tying this specifically to narrative theory.

Several parts of the definition (e.g., “understanding how presenting information as a narrative can shape audience…”) are not stated in the packet as what narrative theory specifically is, making the requested sense of the term only indirectly implied rather than supported.

The packet does not define narrative theory itself; it only says the study integrates elements of the Elaboration Likelihood Model and narrative theory, so attributing this specific framework to the term is unsupported.

The definition generalizes from a broader statement about how linguistic presentation can affect attention, emotion, and cognition, but the packet does not explicitly equate that effect with narrative theory or say that message form is the key feature of the term.
